title: Architecture and Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model Serving, Observability, Performance (ADR)
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Summary:
This consolidated architecture and standards reference provides the canonical guidance for API design, coding and linting expectations, infrastructure and IaC patterns, model-serving contracts, observability instrumentation, performance targets, and the format and sample ADR (Architectural Decision Record) entries used across Redwood Inference. Use this document as the single source of truth for architecture-level decisions and cross-team implementation requirements.

Table of contents:
1) Principles and scope
2) API standards
3) Coding standards
4) Infrastructure and IaC standards
5) Model-serving standards
6) Observability standards
7) Performance targets and load testing
8) ADRs (decision records) and templates
9) Ownership, rollout, and review cadence

1) Principles and scope
- Purpose: Ensure consistency, reliability, and operational readiness for services that make up the Redwood inference platform.
- Scope: Applies to public REST/HTTP APIs, internal microservices, model-serving endpoints, infrastructure-as-code, observability instrumentation, and performance/benchmarking practices.
- Principles: API-first design, backwards-compatibility, observable by default, infrastructure-as-code, immutable artifacts, and safety-first rollouts.

2) API standards
Overview:
- All public service APIs must ship an OpenAPI v3 specification in the repo root under /api/openapi.yaml. Internal service APIs should follow the same conventions and include a minimal "internal" flag in the spec.
Standards:
- Versioning: Use semantic URI versioning: /v1/, /v2/. Breaking changes require a new major path. Deprecation windows must be documented and at least 90 days for public APIs.
- Resource naming: Use plural nouns (e.g., /models/, /deployments/). Use hyphen-separated lower-case words.
- HTTP verbs: Follow REST semantics (GET=read, POST=create, PUT/ PATCH=update, DELETE=delete). Prefer PATCH for partial updates.
- Pagination: Use cursor-based pagination. Standard parameters: ?after=<cursor>&limit=<n>.
- Filtering & sorting: Use query params, e.g., ?status=active&sort=-created_at. Avoid encoding complex filters in path segments.
- Errors: Use application/json error envelope: {"error": {"code": "string", "message": "string", "details": {}}}. Standard error codes: INVALID_ARGUMENT, NOT_FOUND, UNAUTHORIZED, PERMISSION_DENIED, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, INTERNAL. HTTP codes must map: INVALID_ARGUMENT->400, NOT_FOUND->404, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED->429, INTERNAL->500.
- Idempotency: POST endpoints that create resources must support an Idempotency-Key header for at-least-once client retries where appropriate.
- Security: All APIs require TLS1.2+ and JWT-based auth for service-to-service calls. Public APIs include API key or OAuth2 where applicable.
- Rate limiting: Standard headers for limits: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset.
- Contract tests: Every API must include a lightweight contract test exercised in CI that validates the OpenAPI contract and common error responses.

OpenAPI example (snippet):
---
paths:
  /v1/models:
    get:
      summary: List models
      responses:
        '200':
          description: OK
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/ModelList'
---

3) Coding standards
Languages and style:
- Primary backend languages: Go (services), Python (inference workflows), TypeScript (console/frontend). Use idiomatic style for each language.
- Linters and formatters (enforced in CI):
  - Go: gofmt + golangci-lint (enabled checks: govet, staticcheck, errcheck).
  - Python: black, isort, flake8, mypy (type checking target >= 90% for new code).
  - TypeScript: eslint with recommended rules + prettier.
Testing and review:
- Unit tests: Minimum 80% coverage for new packages.
- Integration tests: Every service must include an integration test run in CI that validates happy-path and one failure mode.
- PR requirements: All PRs must include a description, test plan, linked ADR if applicable, and at least one approving reviewer from an owning team.
- Code comments: Use docstrings for public functions and methods; exported types require clear comments.

4) Infrastructure and IaC standards
- IaC: All cloud resources must be defined in Terraform modules living under infra/ and follow Redwood's module conventions. No ad-hoc console changes.
- Environments: dev -> staging -> prod. Promotion via pipeline only.
- Secrets: Use KMS-backed secrets store (HashiCorp Vault or cloud-native KMS). No plaintext secrets in repos.
- Networking: Services should be deployed in private subnets with minimal public exposure. Use service mesh or mTLS for service-to-service auth (TBD per deployment mode).
- Cost controls: Tagging policy required for all resources: {team, service, environment, cost-center}. Enforce via policy as code.
- CI/CD: Every service pipeline must produce an immutable artifact (container image with digest) and publish to the registry. Deployments must reference image digests, not tags.

Recommended Terraform module table (described):
- module/network: VPC, subnets, route tables, NAT
- module/gke/k8s-cluster OR module/k8s-cluster: cluster config and node pools
- module/iam: roles, policies, service accounts
- module/storage: s3/gcs buckets with lifecycle policies

5) Model-serving standards
Model package and artifactization:
- Models must be checked in to artifact storage with immutable URIs and metadata (model-id, version, framework, quantization-profile).
- Packaging: Every model version includes a manifest.json with fields: model_id, version, framework, parameters, quantization_profile, checksum, export_date.
Serving contract:
- All model-serving endpoints must expose a health endpoint (/live, /ready) compatible with k8s probes.
- Latency hints: Model metadata must include expected p50/p95 latency for a standardized request shape (e.g., 1024 tokens).
- KV cache compatibility: For autoregressive models, ensure KV cache format is versioned and backward-compatible.
- Quantization profiles: Define and store quantization profile name used during packaging (e.g., q4_0, q5_0, fp16). Include fallback policy for lower-precision variants.
Rollouts and compatibility:
- Canary policy: Default canary is 5% traffic for 24 hours with automated metrics checks (error rate, latency, token loss).
- Fallback: Automatic fallback to previous stable model if error rate > 2% or p95 latency regresses by > 50% vs baseline.
- Model approval: Models must pass a suite of evals (accuracy, safety checks) before being promoted from staging.

Model-serving config sample (YAML):
---
model_id: redwood-open-7b
version: 2026-02-01
quantization_profile: q4_0
expected_latency_p95_ms: "1200"
health_endpoints:
  - /live
  - /ready
---

6) Observability standards
- Instrumentation by default: All services must emit structured logs (JSON), metrics, and traces. Use the platform telemetry library for consistent keys and tagging.
- Tracing: Use OpenTelemetry (OTel) tracing with service name, span names, and standard attributes (http.method, http.route, net.peer.ip). Sample rate configurable per environment.
- Metrics: Expose Prometheus-compatible metrics. Standard metrics: request_duration_seconds (histogram), request_count (counter), request_errors_total (counter), model_inference_latency_seconds (histogram), kv_cache_hit_ratio (gauge).
- Logs: Structured logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, trace_id, span_id, request_id, message, extra (JSON). No PII in logs.
- Dashboards: Each critical service must have a per-service dashboard with p50/p95 latency, error rate, throughput, CPU/memory, and model-specific metrics.
- Alerts and SLOs: Define alerts that map to oncall runbooks. Use alert thresholds conservative enough to avoid alert fatigue.

Example Prometheus rule (text):
- alert: HighModelLatency
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(model_inference_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service)) > 1.2
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: page
  annotations:
    summary: "p95 model latency is high for {{ $labels.service }}"

7) Performance targets and load testing
- Platform SLOs (guideline):
  - API control-plane endpoints: p50 < 50ms, p95 < 200ms (where feasible).
  - Model inference hosted (small models, <7B): p50 < 150ms, p95 < 600ms.
  - Large models (>7B): targets should be documented per-model.
- Load testing: Use standardized harness (eng-serving-runtime/benchmark-suite). Tests to run in performance CI: sustained throughput test (1h), spike test (5x baseline), and resource-scaling test.
- Benchmark reporting: Every performance run must include: test configuration, artifact digests, cluster config, and raw traces. Store results in the perf DB with metadata for trend analysis.

8) ADRs (Architectural Decision Records)
- Format: Use the ADR template stored at /docs/adr-template.md. ADRs are small markdown files stored under docs/adrs/ in the repo.
- Required ADR fields (must be present and are required by reviewers): id, title, status (proposed|accepted|deprecated), context, decision, consequences, date, authors.
- Canonical indexing: Add a link to the central Confluence index when ADR is created.

Sample ADR (text):
---
id: ADR-2026-03
title: Standardize on OpenTelemetry for traces and metrics
status: accepted
date: 2026-02-20
authors: ["Ava Martinez"]
context: Multiple teams were using different vendor SDKs and metrics formats leading to high maintenance costs.
decision: Adopt OpenTelemetry for traces and metrics; provide a platform shim library that implements OTel and exports to the platform backend.
consequences: Unified telemetry, easier cross-service traceability, migration effort required for all teams.
---

9) Ownership, rollout, and review cadence
- Ownership: The architecture-and-standards working group owns this document; primary contacts: Ava Martinez (runtime), Ethan Chen (infra).
- Review cadence: Biannual review of this document or earlier if a major platform change occurs.
- Change process: Propose changes via ADR. Small clarifications can be PRs on repo docs; material changes require an ADR and review by at least two reviewers including one infra owner.

Appendix: ADR template snippet and OpenAPI checklist
- ADR checklist: impact analysis, rollback plan, telemetry changes, security considerations, test plan.
- OpenAPI checklist: spec present in repo, contract tests in CI, authentication documented, error model documented, example requests/responses provided.

Operational runbook excerpt (when oncall page fires HighModelLatency):
1) Acknowledge page and open the model-serving dashboard.
2) Check p95 latency, error rate, and recent deploys.
3) If a recent model or infra deploy occurred in last 30 minutes, roll back to previous image digest.
4) If not deploy-related, scale up probe workers or increase burst pool (for dedicated clusters) and notify SRE.
5) Postmortem: write a short incident summary within 72 hours and link ADRs if root cause requires a standards change.

Contact and references:
- Working group page: confluence://architecture-and-standards/working-group
- ADR template: docs/adrs/adr-template.md
- Perf harness: eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- Telemetry library: eng-platform/sdks/telemetry

This document is intended to be actionable and referenced directly in PRs, runbooks, and onboarding. Update the related ADRs list whenever a new significant platform decision is made.
